question: Towards the end of 2025, President Zelenskyy’s inner circle was hit by a string of corruption scandals, leading Andriy Yermak to resign and exposing misappropriation of huge funds in the Energoatom affair. At the same time, the EU is committing EUR 50 billion to the Ukraine Facility, funding which is strictly contingent on upholding the rule of law and effectively combating corruption. 1.

Given the seriousness of the matter, is it the Commission’s view that the rule of law continues to be upheld, or does it intend to activate the mechanism for suspending payments to freeze the next quarterly instalment until it has got to the bottom of these affairs?

Given that the scandal revolves around the nuclear operator and the Ministry of Energy, what specific assurances can the Commission give that no EU funding has been funnelled through any entities or subcontractors subject to investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine?

Given the wave of resignations we have seen, which point to a potential failure on the part of the European Court of Auditors, does the Commission intend to launch an external, independent audit of the funding provided since 2024 so as not to have to rely on reports from the Ukrainian authorities?

answer: The Commission is closely monitoring corruption allegations and the investigation in the energy sector by Ukraine’s anticorruption institutions. The investigation shows that the anti-corruption bodies are functioning in Ukraine. Fighting corruption requires continuous efforts, and recent developments confirm Ukraine’s commitment.

All payments from the Ukraine Facility are made under the precondition that Ukraine continues to uphold and respect effective democratic mechanisms, including a multi-party parliamentary system and the rule of law, and to guarantee respect for human rights. Respect for the rule of law includes the fight against corruption.

If this precondition is not met, the Commission submits a proposal to the Council to suspend the payments until the precondition is again met, regardless of reform progress. For each payment, the Commission conducts a detailed assessment. So far, the precondition has always been deemed fulfilled, including for the 6th disbursement of around EUR 2.

3 billion made under the Ukraine Plan (Pillar I of the Ukraine Facility) on 22 December 2025 (1). Under the Ukraine Facility, Ukraine must also fulfil specific reforms to receive instalments and ensure the integrity of all energy-related financial support, including by following up on corruption allegations.

In the EU accession process, Ukraine must strengthen anti-corruption and financial control institutions, corporate governance in state-owned enterprises and public procurement to mitigate corruption risks. These priorities were reaffirmed in the Joint Statement between Commissioner for Enlargement and Deputy Prime Minister of Ukraine of 11 December 2025, which sets out ten key reforms (2).

This question is supported by Members other than the authors: Julien Leonardelli (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Thierry Mariani (PfE), Volker Schnurrbusch (ESN). https://enlargement.ec.europa.eu/news/eu-releases-eu23-billion-support-ukraines-financial-needs-2025-12-22_en . https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/es/statement_25_3030 .

All EU financial support includes anti-fraud measures, with funds strictly monitored and corrective action taken if needed. Expenditures under the Ukraine Facility are overseen by the independent Ukraine Facility Audit Board, which supports the Commission through regular on-site audits and coordination with Ukrainian authorities. To date, there is no evidence of funds diverted for unintended purposes.
